Whether you’ve been in sales for five days or five decades, success has always come down to one simple question: Was it a conversation worth having?

There’s a lot of discussion right now about seller productivity.

How do we help reps move faster?
How do we automate more outreach?
How do we use AI to generate more activity?

Fair questions. Speed matters.

But I wonder if we’ve become so focused on optimizing the sales motion that we’ve stopped asking how it feels to be on the receiving end of it.

Most buyers are overwhelmed by AI-generated emails and automated follow-ups that all start to sound the same. Efficiency for the seller doesn’t automatically create value for the buyer.

The next phase of Revenue AI won’t be defined by who generates the most activity. It’ll be defined by who helps revenue teams engage with more precision, context, and a genuine understanding of the customer’s business.

That’s what we’re building toward with the Predictive Revenue System at Clari + Salesloft. Separating signal from noise.

Because buyers won’t remember how automated your process was, but they will remember if the conversation was worth having.

posts.content:
I got the AI summary from a call I had last week, and the first five minutes read like this: "The team discussed their love for Animal Kingdom, Outlast, Widow's Bay, and The Watcher."

My first reaction was mild amusement. Five minutes of a business call, summarized and logged, spent on TV show recommendations.

But that call turned out to be one of the more productive ones I've had in weeks. The agenda items we eventually got to turned out to be some of the best work we've done together. The conversation felt different: less performative, and more like three people actually trying to solve a problem rather than running through a deck.

The next day, one of those people sent me a Slack letting me know my audio had been cutting in and out on a larger call. They flagged it quietly and early, without being asked.

Stick with me here because I do think these things are connected. When people trust you, their instinct is to tell you what's actually going on…the real risk, the honest read, the thing nobody else will say.

None of that happens in a call that goes straight to slide one.

The summary captured the five minutes of TV talk; what it couldn't capture is what those five minutes made possible.

posts.content:
Something I've been thinking about lately: are we heading toward a moment where companies run out of things to build?

Not because innovation dries up, but because the backlog of features customers haven't finished absorbing yet is outpacing the ones worth shipping next. You slow the releases down to let adoption catch up. And then the pipeline runs dry.

To me, it's having your favorite band release an album every day. Sounds incredible in theory, until you realize you haven't finished listening to the last one, and the one before that is already a distant memory. The music isn't the problem...the pace is.

AI has made it faster than ever to build technology, but it hasn't changed how long it takes for people to actually adjust how they work. The responsibility that comes with that speed is knowing when to slow down.

Speed is only an advantage if the people on the other end can keep up.

posts.content:
We talk a lot in this industry about what AI can do. So we ran the numbers and looked at 12 weeks of usage across 40,000 sellers.

The top 10% of Salesloft users generate 4x more pipeline and 8x more meetings than the bottom 10%. A gap that wide usually points to something 

more systemic than talent or effort alone.

A few things worth highlighting:

- Consistency beats intensity: Sellers who use the platform every week generate 4x the pipeline and 7.5x the meetings of sporadic users. Showing up systematically outperforms showing up occasionally at full throttle.
- Platform depth compounds: Sellers using seven products generate roughly 9x the weekly activity of those on one. The more of the system you use, the more the system works for you.
- AI users operate at a different level: Person Research users made nearly 3x as many calls as non-users.
- The role gap is significant: For Mid-Market full-cycle sellers, the performance gap between the highest and lowest users stretches to 8.7x. That's an adoption opportunity sitting inside most revenue teams right now.
- Underuse has a real cost: The modelled gap for customers is around $1M per seller per year in pipeline already within reach.

Read the full findings here: https://lnkd.in/enA9mpwf

Shadow IT almost broke enterprise tech in the 2010s. And now, shadow AI has the ability to do the same thing to revenue.

As someone who came up through IT, I say this with some authority. I've seen firsthand what happens when teams move fast without a shared foundation. The sprawl, the conflicting data, and the 2 am calls when something mission-critical breaks because nobody knew what was actually running.

I get it though, everyone has their pet AI model. The one they swear by. The one that "just works" for them. And GTM teams, more than anyone, are wired to adopt fast.

In the SaaS era, that meant a new tool every quarter. But in the AI era, it's a different problem entirely.

The fix isn't a governance memo. It's architecture. Revenue AI only works when it's connected: One system, one data layer, one version of what's actually happening in the business.

Shadow IT taught us that speed without foundation creates chaos. Shadow AI will teach us the same lesson. The question is whether we learn it the easy way or the hard way.

posts.content:
A story broke recently about a company that accidentally spent $500 million on AI in a single month. Not through a strategic initiative. Through unrestricted access, no usage controls, and the assumption that lower token costs meant lower risk. 

As a lifelong Simpsons fan, it immediately made me think of Homer Simpson's backyard BBQ project. The tools were all there, but the outcome was not what anyone had in mind.

And from what's being reported, this is far from an isolated incident.

I'm a genuine believer in experimentation with AI. The teams learning by doing it right now are building instincts that will compound for years. Sitting on the sidelines waiting for the perfect strategy is its own kind of risk.

But this is where the build vs. buy conversation gets interesting. Tokens costs in some organizations are getting out of control but the ability for anyone build whatever they want is compelling. That logic makes sense at the starting line. What it misses is everything that comes after: maintaining it, upgrading it, securing it, and governing who can use it. Token costs at scale compound in ways that rarely show up in the original estimate.

The question isn't whether you can build it. The question is whether you want to own everything that comes with it.

Something one of my newer colleagues and I were talking about last week got me thinking.

I don't know a single person who does only what their job title says. Not one. The best people I've worked with have always done far more than their description: they've filled gaps, learned things outside their lane, and solved problems nobody formally assigned to them. The title was always just a rough approximation of the person.

Early in most careers, titles matter enormously. They signal our status and shape how we see ourselves. But some of the best leaders I've worked with are the ones who decided to stop chasing the title and start chasing the problem instead.

Many organizations, including ours, are facing a version of this now. As AI changes what work actually looks like, there's a temptation to solve for it by creating new titles like Chief AI Officer, GTM Engineer, Revenue Architect...the list is growing.

But titling people to solve a problem isn't the same as skilling them to solve a problem. One is organizational housekeeping, while the other is genuine transformation.

What we're focused on is the second. When agents are doing more of the execution, what matters is what your people can actually do and the outcomes they drive. Not what it says on the org chart.

I've been in a lot of planning conversations over the past few weeks as our team maps out 2026. And four priorities are clearly defining how we operate and invest.

1. AI that drives revenue, not headlines
AI only matters if it improves how the revenue engine runs. More accurate forecasts. Better deal inspection. Smarter customer engagement. The bar is simple: does it help us drive predictable growth?

2. Durable, disciplined revenue growth
Right now, the focus is on strengthening what already works. Expanding into the right markets. Improving conversion. Protecting retention. In this environment, predictable growth beats flashy bets. That only happens when marketing, sales, customer success, and finance are operating as one team.

3. Financial rigor as a competitive advantage
In a volatile market, you cannot afford surprises. You need to know exactly what's happening in your pipeline, where deals are slipping, and where retention risk is building. The teams that win are the ones operating from the same set of numbers.

4. Strategic agility built into the operating model.
If your revenue teams are operating from different signals, you lose time. Alignment and a single source of truth are what let you adjust quickly without creating chaos. 

None of these priorities stand alone. Agility is what makes them work together.

In 2026 and beyond, the advantage will go to the companies that run their revenue engine with clarity, alignment, and precision.

posts.content:
"Will it make the boat go faster?"

At the recent Clari + Salesloft RKO, we heard from Ben Hunt-Davis MBE, Olympic gold medalist and author of the book by the same name.

His team had one filter for every decision on their path to gold: "Will it make the boat go faster?"

Simple. But not easy to live by.

I'm 100 days into the CEO role at Clari + Salesloft. Everything is new, priorities are immediate, and expectations are real. There's no shortage of things pulling for your attention, and early on, the instinct is to say yes to most of them.

What I keep coming back to is exactly this: not doing more, but doing the right things.

The metaphor of 'making the boat go faster' is deceptively sharp. Every choice, every initiative, every distraction: does it actually move you forward? If the answer is no, that's information. The discipline isn't just knowing your goal. It's being willing to cut what doesn't serve it, even when it feels productive.

That kind of clarity is hard to practice. But I think it's what separates good teams from great ones.

Thank you, Ben Hunt-Davis MBE, for the perspective and inspiration.

Most enterprise leaders are wrestling with the same question: Where's the ROI on our AI investment? It's a fair question. Budgets have gone in, expectations have been set, and for a lot of organizations the returns are harder to point to than the spend.

One of the more interesting things happening inside Clari + Salesloft right now is that the AI conversation has stopped being a technology conversation and started being an everyone conversation.

It's not just the revenue teams experimenting with what's possible. It's marketing, product, engineering, HR, finance; every function finding its own version of the problem AI can help solve. And every function learning something the others haven't figured out yet. 

What's become clear is that the value isn't just in what any one team discovers, but what happens when those discoveries start to travel.

A prompt that saves an engineer two hours of documentation work turns out to be useful for a CSM writing account summaries. A workflow a marketer built for campaign analysis turns out to have an application in sales coaching. 

The learning compounds in ways that nobody planned for, and faster than any top-down rollout could have engineered.

I think this is actually how AI value gets realized at scale: through the accumulation of small, practical discoveries that get shared across functions by people who are genuinely curious and willing to say "here's what I tried, here's what worked, and here's what didn't." That kind of organizational honesty is harder to build than the technology, and worth more when you have it.

We're still early, but the signal is encouraging. The investment starts paying back when the learning stops living in silos.

Last week I spent time with our leadership team at an offsite. It reinforced how much the nature of leadership has evolved in recent years.

For a long time, leadership scale came from direct oversight. Hire strong people. Set clear activity expectations. Review performance closely. That approach worked well when organizations were smaller and systems were simpler.

Today, work flows across more tools, more data, and more handoffs than ever before. In that environment, outcomes are shaped less by individual effort alone and more by how thoughtfully the system is designed.

Where leaders create the most leverage now is clarity; on priorities; in the signals teams use to guide decisions; and in how work should move when speed matters.

Revenue leaders often see this first, but the principle applies across the organization. The role of leadership is increasingly about designing the conditions for success and making it easier for teams to do their best work every day.

Organizations that get this right will scale more effectively, deliver stronger results, and build teams that perform well over time.

Productivity and predictability are not the same muscle. But nost organizations have only ever trained one of them.

article.subtitle: toplinemedia.substack.com

posts.content:
Yesterday, a senior leader who recently joined Clari + Salesloft told me he'd never worked somewhere with so few weekend calls.

I told him that wasn't an accident, it’s a design choice.

I keep a lunch break on my calendar. I don't send late-night emails or message people when they're offline. If someone's running a few minutes late to a call, we don't sweat it. 

Some will read that and assume it comes at the expense of performance. In my experience, the opposite is true.

We've romanticized busyness in go-to-market for years. Long hours became a proxy for commitment; we'd see the lights on late and call it dedication. In reality, it's often a signal the system isn't working.

The best revenue organizations are intense, sure, but not chaotic. They move quickly because they're clear, not because they're constantly online.

High performance should feel deliberate. And occasionally, it should include lunch.

Lately, I’ve been thinking a lot about my days in Customer Support. Even as CEO, that perspective still shapes how I see the business.

Support gives you a very real view of how growth actually happens. You’re there when something breaks. When expectations aren’t met. When customers are frustrated, under pressure, and looking for answers. You learn quickly that trust is built or lost in those moments.

When customers feel supported, heard, and confident problems will get resolved, they stick around. When they don’t, growth slows fast, no matter how strong the pipeline looks.

That time in Support changed how I have shown up throughout my career. You’re closest to the customer’s reality. You hear friction as it’s happening. You see how complexity creeps in and how often teams are asked to deliver results with limited visibility and constant urgency.

That way of thinking never really leaves you.

It’s also how we approach revenue at Clari + Salesloft:

- Anchor decisions in real customer experience
- Eliminate friction that quietly erodes trust
- Follow through, every time

I still run decisions through a simple filter: Will this make it easier to resolve problems? Will it help teams act with confidence? Will customers feel the difference when it counts?

Titles may change, but the responsibility does not. Leading with a support mindset is still the best way I know to build trust, create value, and drive real growth. 🚀

Modern revenue teams are complicated. Four generations. Different ways of working. A growing stack of sales technology.

The result is friction, and it’s expensive.

New research from Clari and Salesloft shows generational conflict is quietly draining nearly $56 billion in productivity from U.S. sales teams every year. Not because sellers aren’t talented. Because teams struggle to align on how work actually gets done.

A few data points that really stood out:

-85% of sellers say AI tools improve performance and work-life balance
-Nearly two-thirds aren’t using those tools to their full potential
-Sellers on cross-generational teams lose 5+ hours a week to miscommunication and duplicated effort
-Almost 40% of Gen Z sellers say they’d rather be managed by AI than by a Baby Boomer

That last one is not about loving automation. It’s about broken working relationships.

Here’s the opportunity most teams are missing. When experienced sellers and newer reps actually learn from each other, magic happens. Pattern recognition meets digital fluency. Judgment meets speed. Relationships meet scale.

AI does not replace sellers. Sellers who know how to use AI have the edge.

The real work for leaders right now is human. Enablement over enforcement. Mentorship that flows both ways. Technology that bridges gaps instead of widening them.

We put all the data and practical takeaways into our latest report, “The $56B Cost of Generational Conflict and How AI Can Fix It.”

And while this research is grounded in sales, the takeaway applies far beyond it. Any workplace with multiple generations, evolving tools, and pressure to perform is facing the same tension.

How leaders handle it will determine whether that friction becomes a drag on productivity or a real competitive advantage.

There’s a difference between having a meeting and having the real meeting.

Most teams get through the agenda, but what matters usually sits just underneath it: the hesitation behind a number or the concern someone almost didn’t say out loud. 

When that stays unspoken, alignment starts to slip even if everything looks fine in the room, and those gaps tend to show up later in execution.

That’s why I push my team to challenge each other and debate openly. We have the meeting in the meeting and say the hard things directly, because the business deserves that level of honesty. It’s not always comfortable, but it leads to clearer decisions and fewer surprises down the line.

That approach has shaped how I lead, and it’s becoming the standard across Clari + Salesloft . No protected silos, no side conversations after the fact, just a shared commitment to getting to the truth together.

The best teams lean into the tension, stay honest with each other, and work through it in the moment, because that’s where real alignment comes from.

Spent time with our London team yesterday, including a sharp session hosted by Becci O'Shea. A few things landed hard:

You can't fake proximity to the product. 
When you operate inside the same system you bring to customers, you stop talking about features and start obsessing over outcomes. The gap between what you say and what you know closes fast.

Being busy doesn't equal progress. 
The bar I hold myself to: be in the room to contribute or to learn. If neither is happening, leave. Focus is a discipline most leaders underinvest in.

Ego is a tax on execution.
Remove it and clarity improves, decisions accelerate, trust compounds. You feel it immediately in rooms where people are more aligned on the outcome instead of the credit.

What stood out wasn't just the conversation, it was the mindset. A team that understands the direction, stays close to the problem, and is committed to changing how revenue runs.

That combination is rare, and it's what turns strategy into results.
